title: Coding Adventure: Simulating Fluids
beats: Draw one circle, add gravity, velocity, box collision and damping; each step is run and watched
Scale to an array of particles in a grid; run it and watch them collapse onto each other
Name the problem (overlap), admit the maths is over his head, set a modest goal: a rough starting point
Blur the few particles into a continuous density field (smoothed particle idea) with a radius of influence
Draw the influence-vs-distance graph, try linear, cubed, squared-radius kernels; pick by playing around
Write the density function: sum of mass times influence
Test on a uniform grid: raising the radius should only blur but density explodes
Reinterpret influence as heights times box area = volume; normalise kernel volume to 1; verify 187 stays constant
Liquids are incompressible so push particles from high to low density; needs a gradient
Step back to an abstract made-up 2D function approximated by particles to understand the machinery
Approximation is exaggerated where particles are dense; fix by dividing by density
Reveal the core SPH equation after the code works; substitute density for A and it collapses to the earlier formula
Gradient by finite differences: step in x and y, divide by step; arrows drawn, 20 s per frame
Fast gradient: direction toward the particle, steepness from the kernel slope; sum of per-particle gradients; sign wrong, fix by trial
Cache densities after realising calculateDensity loops all particles: 5 s down to 18 ms; says he should have started there
Target density, pressure multiplier, pressure from density error; admits it models gas more than liquid; colour-code pressure
Force to acceleration: use density not mass because volume element; NaN from self-distance, then wrong sign twice
Remove inertia (assign acceleration directly) to isolate the problem; kernel is too flat at close range so swap to spiky kernel
Behaviour worsens over time; Newton's third law motivates a shared (averaged) pressure
Few thousand particles gives 5 fps; need to skip far particles using a grid with cell size equal to smoothing radius (3x3 cells)
Spatial hash on a 10-entry example: cell coordinate, prime hash, key, sort, start-index array, lookup walk-through
Hash collisions waste time but distance check fixes correctness; code shown; 5 fps to 120
Pressure-multiplier ramp hack, then predicted positions: first thinks no effect, then big effect
Grid of sims at 60 to 1000 steps/s shows timestep dependence; remove delta time for consistent look-ahead
Add mouse push/pull interaction and gravity; pick up a ball of water and drop it
Half an hour in, only made points that dislike being too close or too far, yet fluid behaviour emerges
Show Navier-Stokes; map terms to what has been built; viscosity term replaced by a simple velocity-blurring version
Try viscosity 5 (too high), 0.5 (good), then a side-by-side comparison grid
Clamping negative pressure removes droplets but makes rain; negative pressure was acting as crude surface tension; undo and add near-pressure
Jelly-like bounce; stiffness fix costs more steps per frame; defer to future
Move to GPU compute shader for parallel tiny tasks
Bitonic merge sort on 16 lines with random values; compare-swap pairs in parallel, stage by stage
Scale up 100 to 40,000 particles, obstacle level-out test
Extend to 3D by float2 to float3, rescale kernels, transform bounding box
Wishlist: stability, less finicky parameters, boundaries, boats, raymarched rendering

metrics.key_term: smoothed particle hydrodynamics (smoothing kernel, density, pressure gradient)
metrics.misconception: yes: raising smoothing radius on a uniform grid should leave density unchanged but it explodes (5:57-6:13), also a gas-style pressure used for a liquid, flagged as a caveat
metrics.brute_force: yes 0:21: single particle, then particle array and naive all-pairs loops; finite-difference gradient at 11:57 (20 s per frame); each followed by optimisation
metrics.examples: 4 or 5 progressive worlds: 1 particle, grid of particles, random cloud, abstract made-up function, 10-slot hash example, 16-line sorting network; then 100 to 40k particles and 3D
metrics.ending: Admits the fluid is unrealistic, lists a wishlist, teases rendering and boats; no recap of the whole, process-diary close

theory: The video teaches by letting the learner watch someone fail forward in public: each concept enters only when a visible bug demands it, and the maths arrives as the name for something already working. Honesty about not understanding (and about being wrong) works as a pacing device and makes the learner trust the next step. Stepping stones are invented freely, including a meaningless toy function and a 10-slot hash example, whenever the real problem is too tangled.
velocity: Scene builder: support a break-it-first mode where the sim visibly fails (collapse, density explosion) before the concept is introduced, with the failure state reusable as the later success comparison
Orchestrator: allow a stepping-stone detour playbook (abstract made-up function) when learner model shows confusion on the real problem, then return with a callback
Voice: tutor may admit mistakes and 'should have done this first' moments; add a presenter-error tag so evals can count them
Ghost hands: sliders and parameter grids (viscosity 0, 0.5, 5; step counts) driven by the tutor so the learner sees the effect of each knob side by side
Learner model: reveal equation after the learner has produced it in code or on screen; test with a special case substitution
Evals: check that notation appears after a working visual and that every simplification is paired with a stated caveat
